text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft, a few questions. Each answer changes what goes in the letter.

1. **Names and addressee.** What is Tomás's last name, and what are your name, the farm's name and its location? Is the letter going to a named person or the admissions committee, and is there a deadline? I won't make up names or details.

2. **His written English.** This is the first thing an admissions reader will worry about in a two-year program with coursework. What can you tell them? How long has he been in the night class, and have you noticed any change? Does he do any writing on the job, like entering notes in the herd software or leaving shift logs? That would show he already handles written work.

3. **The 5 weeks away.** You told me about it, so I'm guessing you want it in the letter. Handled well, it reads as a family emergency, not a reliability problem. To write it that way, I need to know how it ended. Did he come back when he said he would? Did you keep his job open? Did he do anything to help cover his shift before he left? If you'd rather leave it out, tell me.

4. **The mastitis cases.** What did catching 9 cases early save the farm? Animals kept in the herd, milk not thrown out, lower vet bills? Even a rough figure helps. Also, did he learn the software on his own, or did you train him?

5. **What you'll commit to.** Would you hire him back after the program, or keep him on part-time while he studies? A manager who wants the person back is one of the strongest things a reference can say. I'll only include it if you'll stand behind it.

6. **Anything else.** Is there anything an admissions committee might find out from his application or interview that I should address, or anything that would make the letter stronger? For example, training newer workers, other jobs he does, or how he gets along with the vet.

1. Tomás Reyes. I'm Mike Hollis, farm manager at Hollis Dairy. Letter goes to the admissions committee, through the college's online portal. Due February 1.

2. I don't know exactly how long he's been in the class, or whether he writes notes in the software or shift logs.

3. Keep it in. Before he left he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would.

4. The vet said catching them early saved us about $8,000. I don't know if he learned the software on his own or got trained.

5. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program. I can also take a phone call from the committee, 555-0187. I can't promise anything after the program, and I can't pay any of his tuition.

6. He failed the written test in a dairy safety course once and passed it the second time.

I've written it as a recommendation for admission. The letter mentions both weak spots you told me about, the written English and the five weeks away, and answers each one with what you know about how he handled it.

<final_document>
To the Admissions Committee:

I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow dairy farm. I am writing to recommend Tomás Reyes for your two-year agricultural technology program. Tomás has worked for us for three years, since he was 19. He already does technical work with livestock, and he has shown he can learn new systems on the job.

Tomás runs our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, five days a week. He also learned our herd management software and now uses it to flag sick cows for our vet. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early, and our vet estimates that catching them early saved us about $8,000. That is the kind of work your program trains people for, and he is already doing it.

He is dependable. In three years he has missed two shifts. The one long absence came last summer, when his father fell sick in Mexico and Tomás was away for five weeks. He told me two days before he left. In those two days he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would. I count the way he handled that as a mark in his favor.

You should know that his written English is weaker than his spoken English. He knows it, and he is taking a night class to improve it. He once failed the written test in a dairy safety course. He did not let that stop him: he took it again and passed.

While he is in your program, I will keep his job open for him part-time on weekends, so he can keep working while he studies. I am glad to talk with anyone on the committee about him. You can reach me at 555-0187.

I recommend Tomás strongly.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
555-0187
</final_document>

A few notes:

- **Left out on purpose:** I didn't mention tuition or what happens after the program. Saying you can't help with those wouldn't help him, and the committee won't expect you to.
- **Worth adding if you can find out:** how long he's been in the night class. "He has been taking it since [month]" would make that paragraph stronger. It's an easy thing to ask him.
- **Not included:** I didn't add a date, farm address or letterhead because I don't have them. Add them if the portal asks for a formatted letter.
- **Check before sending:** the line "I count the way he handled that as a mark in his favor" is my reading of what you told me. Keep it only if it's true for you.
